title: An online shop for a furniture maker
metaTitle: A furniture shop that shows scale and time
excerpt: Show scale, material, and lead time on the furniture page, with freight before the card. A short checkout still has to tell the truth about delivery.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water. A furniture page has to hold material and lead time with the same care that color holds a shape.
caption: Color holding a shape. The page has to hold the facts. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What three facts belong on a furniture product page immediately?
faqs.answer: Scale, material, and lead time, with the price. Dimensions go in text beside an image of the whole piece. If it is made to order, the weeks belong in that first glance, not after payment. A sofa and a stool should not share a vague delivery line.

faqs.question: When should freight appear?
faqs.answer: Before the card, and as a range on the product page if you can state one. Baymard's research cites extra costs and slow delivery among the reasons people abandon. White-glove versus threshold delivery is part of the product. Do not reveal it as a surprise on the last step.

faqs.question: Who may charge the balance on a made-to-order piece?
faqs.answer: A person, after checking the piece is actually ready, if the balance is due before shipment. A timer that charges because a date arrived will bill for a chair that is still in the workshop. The deposit, the balance, and the timing should be plain before the first payment.

markdown:
A furniture maker ecommerce website has to show scale, material, and lead time before it asks for a large payment. The product page carries those three. Checkout stays short, with freight visible. A marketplace grid of tiny rooms will shrink a chair into a swatch and hide the weeks it takes to make.

Build the page around the piece in a space a buyer can measure, then take the order without pretending you are a warehouse of everything.

## Scale, material, and time on the first screen

The first screen is the piece, large, with the price and the lead time in the same glance. "Made to order, eight to ten weeks" belongs there if that is true. "Ships tomorrow" belongs there only when it does. A sofa and a stool do not share a vague "delivery calculated later." People are buying an object that will not fit in a mailbox, and they are often buying time.

Show scale with a full piece in a room or against a person, and give dimensions in text: width, depth, height, seat height if someone will sit. A photograph suggests size. The numbers are what a buyer uses to decide whether it fits the wall. Put the numbers near the image, not in a downloadable spec sheet as the only source. If there is a clearance or a door the piece must pass through, say the packed or the assembled limit, whichever they need. A beautiful chair that cannot enter the building is a failed page.

Material is the second fact. Wood species, finish, upholstery cloth, what is solid and what is veneer. Name them. "Sustainably crafted" is not a material. If a finish changes the color, the photograph and the name of the finish have to change together. A buyer comparing oil and paint should see both, shot in the same light.

Lead time is a material fact for a small maker. If the queue is long, say the queue. If a piece is in the workshop now, say that, and remove the sentence when it sells. Do not leave "in stock" on a page after the only one has gone. That is a promise you will have to unwind after they have paid.

## A catalog that still feels like one workshop

The collection uses one crop logic. Full pieces, same margin, same kind of room or the same plain sweep. Do not mix a detail of a joint, a wide room, and a close-up of cloth as three neighboring tiles. The thumbnail is the whole piece. Details live on the product page, where someone has already chosen to look.

If you make eight pieces, show eight pieces. Filters for style adjectives will not help. If you make many variants of a table, filter by the decision: size, or wood. Leave "inspiration" categories off. They multiply pages without helping someone measure a doorway.

Related pieces are the bench that belongs with the table, chosen by you, not a price-similar rail. Two is enough. A buyer of a dining table does not need twenty other lives. They need to know whether the bench is the same wood and the same lead time.

Commission work, if you take it, should be a page with a boundary: what you will make, what you need from them, and that a price comes after a conversation. Do not put a fake "add to cart" on a one-off you have not scoped. The cart is for pieces with a price and a lead time you can stand behind.

Hanabi's public work includes shops and brand sites built as specific catalogs rather than borrowed marketplace chrome. The furniture page fails when it imports that chrome: badges, endless recommendations, and a grid that treats a chair as a unit of content.

## Variants, cloth, and the picture that must swap

Size variants need their own dimensions, not one image stretched in the buyer's imagination. If the eight-foot table is a different proportion from the six-foot, show both or say clearly that the photograph is the six-foot and the longer top changes by a stated amount. Silence here becomes a dispute at delivery.

Upholstery options swap the image. A buyer who selects a striped cloth and still sees the plain one will feel misled even if the checkout text is correct. If you cannot shoot every cloth, show a controlled swatch next to one hero and say that the room photo is the house cloth. Then make the swatch large enough to judge, and name the cloth. A postage-stamp swatch is not a variant.

Wood finishes work the same way. If the walnut and the ash are both real, they both get a frame in the same corner of the workshop or the same window light. Mixed locations per finish will make the finish look like a different design.

Stock and made-to-order should not share a button label. "Add to cart" on a ten-week piece needs the time repeated on the button's line. People do not read a romantic lead paragraph when a familiar button is sitting there. The button's neighborhood is where the truth goes.

## Freight, thresholds, and a short checkout

Shipping a chair is not shipping a shirt. Baymard Institute's [cart abandonment research](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) puts extra costs, including shipping and fees, at 40 percent of US online shoppers who had abandoned, and delivery that felt too slow at 20 percent. Not seeing the total up front is 12 percent. The average documented abandonment rate across the 50 studies in that list is 70.22 percent, and 42 percent of US shoppers abandoned because they were just browsing. The buyers who are ready will still leave if freight appears after they have built an emotional commitment to a sofa.

Show a freight range by region on the product page, and the real figure before payment. If you cannot quote until you know the address, ask for the postal code early, then show the number, then continue. Do not wait until the card field. White-glove, threshold, and "you must be home" are product facts. Say which one they are buying.

Checkout itself can still be short. Email, delivery address, a phone number because someone will actually call about a delivery day, the method they chose, and payment. Baymard's ideal of about 12 to 14 form elements, or 7 to 8 fields, against a US average of 23.48 elements, is a fair target. Do not add a room-planning questionnaire to the payment step. Ask for the doorway constraint as an optional note, not as six required dropdowns.

Guest checkout works for a single piece. An account is reasonable if they need to approve drawings or track a long build. Do not force the account on a stool you ship this week. Forced accounts show up at 18 percent in Baymard's abandonment reasons.

## Damage, deposits, and what you do not automate

A large payment needs a plain statement of the deposit, the balance, and when each is due. If the balance is due before shipment, say so before the first payment. A workflow that charges the balance because a timer elapsed, without a person checking the piece is ready, will charge for a chair that is still in clamps. Keep a person on that charge.

Damage and refusal need a sentence: what you will repair, what counts as a delivery exception, and how fast they should tell you. A furniture return is not a mailer. Do not copy an apparel returns policy onto a bed. Write the one you mean.

Do not show a countdown or "twelve people are viewing this" on a piece you make one at a time. The scarcity is the lead time, already stated. Fake urgency on a ten-week chair is absurd, and careful buyers notice.

[Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is the place to see how a studio presents specific products without a marketplace shell. A furniture shop in that spirit is a few true pages, not a theme with every module turned on.

## The workshop queue and the page

When the queue changes, the lead-time sentence changes. That sentence should be a field the maker can edit. If it requires a developer, it will be wrong for months. Wrong lead times are the central trust problem in this category, more than the typeface.

Drawings and material samples, if you send them, are a step on the page or a note after the order, owned by a person. Do not let a confirmation email promise a sample you do not send. The email repeats the dimensions, the finish, the lead time, and the freight. It matches the page they paid on.

If you sell to the trade, keep trade pricing off the public cart. A code that leaks will meet a retail customer, and you will have a pricing conversation you did not want. A separate list of pieces available to the trade is enough.

## Mobile, doorways, and the next decision

On a phone, the first screen is still the whole piece, not a cropped arm. The dimensions stay in text under it. Pinch-to-zoom can help a joint. It cannot be the only way to see the silhouette. Test the category grid at a small size. If the thumbnail could be any brown rectangle, the crop is too tight or the backgrounds are fighting.

The photographs are a system of their own. [Product photography for a furniture maker](/blog/product-photography-for-a-furniture-maker) is next, because scale and material have to be shot with one crop or this page will be more honest than the grid it came from.
